entities.name: Omar Tiberiades
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abū Ḥafṣ ʿUmar ibn al-Farrukhān al-Ṭabarī, known in the Latin West as Omar Tiberiades, was a pivotal Persian astrologer and architect whose intellectual contributions during the late 8th and early 9th centuries significantly influenced the nascent Islamic scientific tradition and, subsequently, European astrology. Flourishing under the patronage of the Abbasid Caliphate, particularly during the reign of Caliph al-Maʾmūn (r. 813–833 CE), Omar Tiberiades played a crucial role in the House of Wisdom's translation movement, bridging Hellenistic astronomical knowledge with burgeoning Islamic scholarship. His work exemplifies the era's rigorous scientific inquiry, merging theoretical astrology with practical applications in architecture and governance, thereby shaping the intellectual landscape of the early Abbasid Golden Age.

His magnum opus, *Kitāb al-Masāʾil* (Book of Interrogations), became a foundational text for horoscopic astrology, meticulously detailing methodologies for casting and interpreting astrological charts based on the moment a question was posed. This work, translated into Latin by Plato of Tivoli in 1136 CE as *Liber Completus in Iudiciis Stellarum* (The Complete Book on Stellar Judgments), introduced sophisticated Arabic astrological techniques to medieval Europe. Beyond theoretical contributions, Omar Tiberiades was also an accomplished architect, designing structures in Baghdad and likely contributing to the caliphal court's urban planning efforts, though specific projects are less documented than his astrological treatises. His expertise in both celestial mechanics and terrestrial construction underscores the comprehensive, interdisciplinary nature of early Islamic scholarship.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Omar Tiberiades's comprehensive astrological works served as a crucial conduit for transmitting Hellenistic and Persian scientific knowledge to both the Islamic world and later medieval Europe. His *Kitāb al-Masāʾil* became a standard reference, shaping astrological practice and contributing to the reintroduction of complex mathematical and astronomical concepts in the Latin West.
